FIELD NOTES — MATERNAL HEALTH PRACTICES STUDY
Gulf coastal district, March 2024
Compiled by the research team. Not for circulation.

--- Day one ---

Arrived by road after the river crossing at Malalaua. The vehicle needed repair
twice on the way and we lost most of the morning to a broken leaf spring. The
driver knew a workshop in the next settlement and we were moving again by two.
Weather clear, hot by midday, with the usual afternoon build-up over the range.

Set up in the guest house behind the administrative office. Two rooms, shared
water tank, power from the office generator between six and ten in the evening.
The office staff were expecting us; the letter from the provincial health
authority had arrived the previous week.

Unpacked and checked the recording equipment. Both machines working. Spare
batteries counted: fourteen, which should be adequate for the week if we are
disciplined about switching off between conversations. Notebooks and consent
forms laid out for tomorrow.

Evening spent reading back through the protocol. The sequencing of the interview
schedule still feels wrong in the opening section and I expect we will adjust it
after the first conversation.

--- Day two ---

Morning at the district office. The administrative officer walked us through the
current figures and was generous with his time. The district has a resident
population of four hundred and twelve, distributed across three settlements,
with the largest concentration around the wharf. This is down from the last
census; the officer attributed the decline to younger people leaving for Port
Moresby and to two families relocating after the flooding in 2022.

He also gave us the annual return for the health post: attendance figures,
referral counts, and the supply requisition schedule. Photocopied what he was
willing to share. The figures will be useful context for the interview material
even if we do not use them directly.

Afternoon spent walking the settlement. Noted the positions of the water points,
the school, and the two stores. The market operates on Tuesday and Friday.
Fishing boats leave before dawn and return mid-morning; the catch is sold
immediately at the wharf and the beach clears by eleven.

Rain from four o'clock. Worked indoors on the schedule revisions.

--- Day three ---

First conversations today. Three in the morning, two after lunch. The revised
opening works better: beginning with the participant's own account of how
practice has changed, rather than with the demographic questions, produced much
fuller responses. Will keep this ordering.

Recording quality good in the guest house room; less good at the health post,
where the generator noise carries. Moved the afternoon conversations to the
veranda.

Transcription is going to be slower than budgeted. Roughly four hours of
transcription per hour of recording at this rate, and we have five hours of
material already. Considering whether to transcribe selectively and return to
the full recordings later.

Consent forms all signed and filed. Reviewed the wording again this evening.
Consent covers use of the responses in research analysis. It does not extend to
publication of individual responses, and two participants asked specifically
whether their words would appear anywhere. Told them no.

--- Day four ---

Weather turned. Heavy rain from before dawn and the road out was impassable by
mid-morning. The river came up quickly and the crossing at Malalaua will be shut
for at least two days according to the office.

Used the time to transcribe. Completed three of yesterday's conversations. The
material on referral decisions is richer than expected and suggests a line of
questioning we had not planned: the reasoning behind when to refer and when to
manage locally seems to rest on a set of judgements that participants find
difficult to articulate directly but describe readily through examples.

Generator failed in the evening. Worked by torchlight until the batteries
demanded rationing, then stopped.

--- Day five ---

Rain continuing but lighter. No conversations scheduled; the participants we had
hoped to see are on the far side of the creek.

Spent the morning on the equipment inventory and the afternoon revising the
coding frame. The categories we brought are too coarse for what we are hearing.
Drafted a revised frame with the referral material as its own axis rather than
folded into the general practice questions.

Long discussion in the evening about whether we are asking the right question at
all. The study was designed around changes in practice over time, but what
participants keep returning to is the difficulty of transport during the wet
season, which shapes every decision they describe. Noted for the analysis.

--- Day six ---

Road still shut. Walked to the far settlement instead, which took two hours each
way along the beach at low tide.

Two conversations there, both good. The second ran to nearly ninety minutes and
would have gone longer had the light held. Battery discipline paid off.

Returning in the dark was a mistake and we will not repeat it. Arranged for the
office driver to collect us next time, tide permitting.

--- Day seven ---

Transcription day. Completed four more.

The material is beginning to cohere. Three themes recur across every
conversation so far: the transport question, the changing role of the health
post relative to home practice, and a generational difference in how younger
women approach the decision to attend.

Our principal informant returned this afternoon of her own accord, having
thought further about a question from Tuesday. She has practised here for
nineteen years, and her account of how the referral relationship with the health
post has evolved over that period is the central material of this study. She was
concerned that her earlier answer had been too brief. We recorded a further
forty minutes.

--- Day eight ---

Follow-up conversations at the health post. Discussed referral patterns in more
detail and the specific difficulty of the wet season crossing. The officer in
charge was helpful about the supply chain and less forthcoming about staffing,
which is understandable.

Equipment inventory recorded and packed. Recordings backed up to both drives and
checked. Fourteen conversations in total, eleven fully transcribed.

Departure arranged for tomorrow morning if the road holds. The office has
offered the vehicle as far as the crossing.

--- Day nine ---

Left at six. Road passable though slow in three places. Crossing at Malalaua
open but running high; waited an hour for the ferry.

Reflections on the way back. The study will need a second visit to cover the
generational material properly, and probably in the dry season. The consent
question will need revisiting before anything is published: what we have is
usable for analysis but not for quotation, and the richest material is precisely
the material that would identify people if quoted.

Filed and stored on return. Backups verified.
